summary: Securus Technologies has trained AI models on years of prison phone calls and is piloting them to monitor inmate communications for planned crimes. The company is using its vast call database to detect criminal activity, but advocates raise concerns about consent and privacy. The FCC has recently allowed telecoms to pass security costs, including AI development, onto inmates, reversing earlier reforms.

claims.text: Securus Technologies trained an AI model on seven years of calls made by inmates in the Texas prison system.
claims.evidence_quote: It created one model, for example, using seven years of calls made by inmates in the Texas prison system

claims.text: Securus has been piloting AI tools to monitor inmate conversations in real time over the past year.
claims.evidence_quote: Over the past year, Elder says, Securus has been piloting the AI tools to monitor inmate conversations in real time.

claims.text: Securus declined to specify where the AI pilot is taking place.
claims.evidence_quote: The company declined to specify where this is taking place

claims.text: Securus's AI model can detect when crimes are being contemplated, allowing intervention earlier in the cycle.
claims.evidence_quote: to detect and understand when crimes are being thought about or contemplated, so that you’re catching it much earlier in the cycle.

claims.text: Inmates and those they call are notified that conversations are recorded, but not that they may be used to train AI.
claims.evidence_quote: People in prison, and those they call, are notified that their conversations are recorded. But this doesn’t mean they’re aware that those conversations could be used to train an AI model

claims.text: Bianca Tylek argues that consent to recording is coercive because inmates have no other way to communicate with family.
claims.evidence_quote: That’s coercive consent; there’s literally no other way you can communicate with your family

claims.text: Inmates in most states pay for calls, so they are charged while their data is collected for AI training.
claims.evidence_quote: not only are you not compensating them for the use of their data, but you’re actually charging them while collecting their data.

claims.text: Securus has a history of improperly recording attorney-client calls, as shown by leaks.
claims.evidence_quote: leaks of its recordings databases showed the company had improperly recorded thousands of calls between inmates and their attorneys.

claims.text: Corene Kendrick says the AI system enables invasive surveillance and courts have set few limits.
claims.evidence_quote: the new AI system enables a system of invasive surveillance, and courts have specified few limits to this power.

claims.text: In 2024, the FCC issued reforms forbidding telecoms from passing recording and surveillance costs to inmates.
claims.evidence_quote: In 2024, the Federal Communications Commission issued a major reform ... that forbade telecoms from passing the costs of recording and surveilling calls on to inmates.

claims.text: In June, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr postponed deadlines for the 2024 reforms and signaled support for using inmate fees to fund AI surveillance.
claims.evidence_quote: In June, Brendan Carr ... said it would postpone all deadlines for jails and prisons to adopt the 2024 reforms, and even signaled that the agency wants to help telecom companies fund their AI surveillance efforts with the fees paid by inmates.

claims.text: On October 28, the FCC voted to allow companies like Securus to pass security costs, including AI development, onto inmates.
claims.evidence_quote: On October 28, the agency went further: It voted to pass new, higher rate caps and allow companies like Securus to pass security costs relating to recording and monitoring of calls—like storing recordings, transcribing them, or building AI tools to analyze such calls, for example—on to inmates.

claims.text: FCC commissioner Anna Gomez dissented, arguing that law enforcement should pay for security costs, not families of incarcerated people.
claims.evidence_quote: Law enforcement should foot the bill for unrelated security and safety costs, not the families of incarcerated people.
